records.title: Vassilis Diakoloukas • 3-й+
records.text: 𝗪𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗘𝘂𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀!! I'm incredibly proud to share that our team won the MathWorks Minidrone Competition Europe! Out of around 70 teams from leading universities across Europe, we made it to the top 5 finalists and earned our place in the grand final at the MathWorks offices in Cambridge, UK. After two days of intense competition, technical challenges, and real-world drone testing, we came home with 1st place! The challenge was to develop a fully autonomous drone capable of navigating an unknown track, making real-time decisions, and landing smoothly and accurately at its destination without relying on a predefined map. Our solution combined computer vision, path planning, and autonomous control. We developed a multi-ring search algorithm to identify the path ahead and determine the drone's direction and speed, along with a trajectory memory mechanism to prevent it from revisiting sections of the track it had already completed. Landing was a challenge of its own. We developed a vision-based algorithm to recognize the landing target, distinguish it from the track, and position the drone accurately above it. But getting everything to work in simulation was only half the job! For the final, we had to adapt our algorithms to run on a real drone with limited onboard processing power, memory, and strict real-time requirements. We redesigned our navigation system around a much lighter single-ring search, reduced the trajectory memory, and simplified the landing approach. The drone could identify the landing target, align itself with its center, lock its horizontal position, and perform a smooth, controlled descent. I've attached a video showing our work in action, from the initial simulation and our multi-ring path planning and trajectory memory algorithms to the final real-world flight. I would like to thank my teammates Athanasios Digkas , Dimitrios Ioannidis , and Marios Antakis for all the hard work and dedication in this incredible experience. I would also like to thank MathWorks and especially Krishna Keerthana Chiruvolu and Manjunath R for organizing the competition and hosting us in Cambridge. It was a fantastic experience and a great opportunity to meet talented students from across Europe! #MathWorks #MinidroneCompetition #Robotics #AutonomousSystems #ComputerVision #AI #Engineering

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or gov
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: SBIR/STTR came back in April after a six-month lapse. The new Strategic Breakthrough Phase II awards can reach $30M, but you have to bring a 100% match from private capital or government sources. Most founders will read that as a fundraising problem. Its an architecture problem first. Whoever writes the matching cheque will ask the same questions a program office would: (1) Is the autonomy behavior separable from the vehicle? A stack hard-wired to one airframes flight controller is a single-platform product. A stack behind a stable vehicle-interface layer can be sold on many platforms. (2) Are the interfaces stable? If every new integration means changing your perception-to-planning boundary, your Phase II cost curve wont stay flat. (3) What does it do when the world stops matching the demo? Degraded sensors, lost links and out-of-distribution scenes should already be characterized, with data. (4) Where does your IP boundary sit? If the value is in the model weights, the training data and the test harness, can you say who holds rights to each? A component with a good demo is a Phase I story. A $30M award means a system with a defined interface, a characterized failure envelope and a clear IP boundary. Start building those before you write the proposal. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

records.title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, n
records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: The Army's Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML) award went out August 31 — $33.4M, roughly a three-year OTA, to Georgia Tech Research Institute. Not Lockheed, not RTX, not Northrop. GTRI is the Weapon Systems Integrator. That's a more interesting choice than it looks. CAML's architecture decouples the autonomous mobility platform from the munitions pallet — you can swap what it fires without redesigning how it moves. That only works if someone owns the interface control documents independent of whoever builds either half. Normally that someone is a prime with decades of vertical-integration leverage. Here it's a research institute whose job is systems engineering, M&S, and acceptance testing — not building either module itself. For a small business building a mobility platform or a munitions pallet for multi-domain fires, this matters more than the dollar figure. The company you have to satisfy technically here isn't your competitor — it's GTRI, judging whether your module's interface conforms to spec. That's a different relationship than the one you're used to with a prime. Before you map the org chart, find out who owns the interface control documents: that's who actually evaluates your product, and they're grading interface compliance, not just capability. Lt. Gen. records.text: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction vanishes the moment it is heard. As a pilot, I witness the operational challenges that come with ATC communications firsthand. Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology. For example the word "stick" near San Francisco is the SSTIK departure, while "stick" in North Carolina is spelled as STIKK. That nuance is not in the audio, and decoding that signal requires more than just good speech recognition. So we built ZEE differently: — A single speech engine that collapses voice activity detection, speaker diarization, and transcription into one model, emitting one speaker-attributed token stream. — Spatial grounding that injects location context so the model correctly transcribes local waypoints and procedures in any airspace. — A language model that decomposes each dense transmission into discrete, structured, verifiable commands. The result: 84% better accuracy than general-purpose speech models on aviation audio, and a 58% reduction in entity transcription errors from spatial grounding. All of it running in real time, offline, and on-device; so that pilots and controllers alike can benefit from this layer of intelligence. Every radio call becomes a permanent, scrollable, time-indexed record. And it lays the foundation for what comes next: catching readback errors and communication breakdowns in real time, before a misheard clearance becomes an incident. The next era of aviation safety should begin where it matters most: in cockpits and air traffic control towers. Preventing tragic, avoidable accidents starts by making communication clear and effortless in the sky. This is one of the missions behind ZEE, and behind everything my extraordinary team builds: a world where every single flight reaches its destination safely. Full post: https://lnkd.in/dvauVg2E.

records.text: Организация Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano разместила контент: How closely do particles follow rotor-induced flow before reaching a blade? New research by Francesco Caccia and Alberto Guardone investigates the dynamics of inertial particles in rotor-induced flows, considering both a wind turbine and a small-scale propeller. The study shows that the key lies in how the particle response time compares with the characteristic time scale of the induced flow. The authors introduce an induction Stokes number to identify the transition between particles that follow the induced velocity field and those that are essentially unaffected by it. A reduced-order analytical model is then developed to capture this delayed particle response, providing corrected conditions for 2-D sectional simulations and reproducing the transition observed in full 3-D simulations. The results have implications for modelling multiphase rotor flows, including applications involving icing and particle-induced erosion. Read On particle dynamics in steady axial rotor flows, published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics: https://lnkd.in/eys6i2qJ #AerospaceEngineering #Polimi.

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have.
